wstep: This card describes hot smoking eel at home with the method of Wisconsin Sea Grant and University of Minnesota Extension, which has been scientifically tested for safety.

akapity: The internal temperature of the fish must reach 160 °F and stay there for at least 30 minutes; if your smoker cannot do this, finish cooking the fish in the oven within 2 hours of smoking.
According to the FDA, gut any fish before salting, drying, pickling or fermenting it.
Even vacuum-packed smoked fish must be kept in the refrigerator or freezer, never at room temperature.
According to Wisconsin Sea Grant, any fish can be smoked, and fatty fish come out juicier than lean fish.
Wisconsin Sea Grant does not name eel among its favorites, but says that any fish can be smoked.
Use only high-quality fish: bad fish that goes into the smoker comes out bad.
Hot smoking to 160 °F takes the fish above 150 °F, the temperature needed to kill parasites, so only fish for cold smoking must be frozen first.
Cold-smoke temperatures are not hot enough to kill bacteria and may even help them grow, so this card covers hot smoking only.
Clean freshly caught fish: gut and gill them, remove the kidney from the belly cavity, and rinse all exposed surfaces with fresh water.
Thaw frozen fish and wash them in fresh water.
The FDA may act against uneviscerated salt-cured, dried or smoked fish more than 5 inches long.
Make the brine from 1 part table salt, not iodized and without anticaking agent, to 7 parts water by volume.
1 cup of salt in 7 cups of water brines 2–3 pounds of fish; for more fish, double the amounts and keep the 1:7 ratio.
Use a plastic or glass container, not a metal one.
Brine in the refrigerator, at 40 °F or below (about 4 °C).
One hour works well in many cases; you can also start with 15 minutes for each half-inch of fish thickness.
Do not let the pieces overlap in the brine.
Do not use recipes with longer brining in a weaker brine: they raise the chance of bacterial growth and are not recommended.
After brining, rinse the surface of the fish.
Place the fish skin-side down on a wire mesh screen, or hang them on hooks or dowels.
Dry the fish with a fan until a smooth, shiny skin called a pellicle forms; on low-humidity days this usually takes 1–2 hours.
Turn fish lying on screens from time to time.
Insert a meat thermometer into the middle of the thickest part of the largest fish, so that it shows the lowest temperature of all the fish.
Put a second thermometer that reads 50–250 °F (about 10–121 °C) through a hole in the smoker to watch the air temperature.
Heat cooks and dries the fish, and smoke gives it flavor and color.
Put the fish in when the air in the smoker reaches about 100 °F (about 38 °C).
Your smoker must be able to reach air temperatures of 200–225 °F (about 93–107 °C).
The internal temperature of the fish must reach 160 °F and stay there for at least 30 minutes.
University of Idaho gives 150–160 °F for at least 30 minutes, while Wisconsin Sea Grant requires 160 °F, so this card uses 160 °F.
With the air at 200–220 °F (about 93–104 °C) the flesh reaches about 160 °F (about 71 °C), but air temperature does not guarantee flesh temperature, so always measure the flesh.
If your smoker cannot heat the fish enough, finish cooking it in the kitchen oven within 2 hours of smoking.
After the fish is cooked, you can let the internal temperature drop to about 125 °F (about 52 °C) and keep smoking for flavor.
A light smoked flavor needs about 8 hours of smoke, and smoking can take up to 12 hours.
Use wood from oak, hickory, maple, alder, beech, apple, white birch or ash.
Do not use pine or other resinous wood, or sawdust from fiberboard or plywood.
Take the fish out of the smoker at once and let it cool at room temperature for about an hour.
Then wrap it in butcher paper or cover it, and refrigerate it.
Keep smoked fish in the refrigerator at 40 °F or below for no longer than 2 weeks, or freeze it for up to 4 months.
Wisconsin Sea Grant allows up to a month in the refrigerator, but this card uses the shorter limit of 2 weeks from University of Idaho.
Smoking does not keep fish from spoiling.
Throw away smoked fish that has been in the refrigerator for more than 2 weeks.
Do not keep smoked fish out of the refrigerator for more than 2 hours, or for more than 1 hour when the temperature is above 90 °F (about 32 °C).

According to the FDA, pregnant women, children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems should avoid refrigerated smoked fish, such as salmon, trout, whitefish or mackerel, except in a cooked dish.
